title: Factors
summary: Give the rider survey's answers an order that means something: make satisfaction a factor with its levels in order, sort bars by how often or how much, combine and lump levels, and compare answers with an ordered factor.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes forcats

steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches forcats, whose functions for factors all start with `fct_`.

steps.title: Text sorts alphabetically

runs.purpose: count the answers to the satisfaction question

steps.explain: `satisfaction` is text, so `count()` sorts it alphabetically: Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, then the two "Very" answers at the end. The answers have an order, from very dissatisfied to very satisfied, but text has no way to know it.

steps.title: Levels set the order: fct()

runs.purpose: list the five answers in their natural order, as `satisfaction_levels`
runs.task: Store the five answers in order, from "Very dissatisfied" to "Very satisfied", in a vector called `satisfaction_levels`.

runs.code:
survey <- survey |>
  mutate(satisfaction = fct(satisfaction, levels = satisfaction_levels))
alternatives: survey = survey |> mutate(satisfaction = factor(satisfaction, levels = satisfaction_levels))
runs.purpose: turn `satisfaction` into a factor with those levels
runs.task: Make `satisfaction` a factor with `fct()` and `levels = satisfaction_levels`, and store the result back in `survey`.

steps.explain: A factor is a variable with a fixed set of possible values, its levels, in an order you choose. `fct()` makes one, and stops with an error if a value isn't among the levels, so a typo can't quietly become `NA`. Now `count()` follows the levels, from very dissatisfied to very satisfied, and the counts read as a scale: {n_satisfied} of the riders are satisfied or very satisfied. The tibble shows the column as `<fct>`.

steps.title: Bars in order: levels and fct_infreq()

runs.purpose: draw a bar for each answer, in the levels' order
runs.task: Draw a bar chart of `satisfaction` with `geom_bar()`.

runs.purpose: draw a bar for each rider's home neighbourhood, ordered by how many riders live there
runs.task: Draw a bar chart with `home_neighbourhood` on the y axis, ordered by frequency with `fct_infreq()`.

steps.explain: ggplot2 draws a factor's bars in the order of its levels, so the satisfaction scale reads left to right. `home_neighbourhood` has no natural order, so the clearest one is by size: `fct_infreq()` puts the most common level first, {top_home}, which ggplot2 draws at the bottom of the y axis. Wrapping it in `fct_rev()` would turn it round. The neighbourhood names on the y axis can be read without turning your head.

steps.title: Order by a value: fct_reorder()

runs.code:
survey |>
  summarize(
    rides = mean(rides_per_week, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = home_neighbourhood
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rides, y = fct_reorder(home_neighbourhood, rides))) +
  geom_point()
alternatives: survey |> group_by(home_neighbourhood) |> summarize(rides = mean(rides_per_week, na.rm = TRUE)) |> ggplot(aes(rides, fct_reorder(home_neighbourhood, rides))) + geom_point()

values.most_home: local({s <- summarize(survey, rides = mean(rides_per_week, na.rm = TRUE), .by = home_neighbourhood); s$home_neighbourhood[which.max(s$rides)]})
values.most_rides: local({s <- summarize(survey, rides = mean(rides_per_week, na.rm = TRUE), .by = home_neighbourhood); format(round(max(s$rides), 1))})

runs.purpose: plot the mean rides per week for each home neighbourhood, ordered by that mean
runs.task: Find the mean `rides_per_week` (`na.rm = TRUE`) for each `home_neighbourhood`, then plot it as points, with the neighbourhoods on the y axis ordered by it: `fct_reorder(home_neighbourhood, rides)`.

steps.explain: `fct_reorder()` orders a factor's levels by another variable, so the points form a line from fewest rides to most and the eye can compare neighbours. In alphabetical order, the same points would zigzag. Riders from {most_home} ride most, {most_rides} times a week on average. With several values per level, `fct_reorder()` orders by their median, or by the function given as `.fun`.

steps.title: Fewer levels: fct_collapse() and fct_lump_n()

runs.code:
survey |>
  mutate(
    feel_safe = fct_collapse(
      agree_feel_safe,
      agree = c("Strongly agree", "Agree"),
      disagree = c("Disagree", "Strongly disagree")
    )
  ) |>
  count(feel_safe)
alternatives: survey |> mutate(feel_safe = fct_collapse(agree_feel_safe, agree = c('Agree', 'Strongly agree'), disagree = c('Strongly disagree', 'Disagree'))) |> count(feel_safe)
runs.purpose: combine the agreement answers into agree and disagree, and count them
runs.task: Add `feel_safe`: `agree_feel_safe` with "Strongly agree" and "Agree" collapsed into `agree`, and "Disagree" and "Strongly disagree" into `disagree`, using `fct_collapse()`. Then count it.

runs.purpose: keep the six most common home neighbourhoods and lump the rest together
runs.task: Count `survey` by `home`: `home_neighbourhood` with all but the 6 most common lumped into "Other", using `fct_lump_n()`.

steps.explain: `fct_collapse()` gives several levels one new name: {n_agree} riders agree that they feel safe, {n_disagree} disagree. Levels not mentioned, such as "Don't know", stay as they are, and missing answers stay `NA`. `fct_recode()` renames single levels the same way. `fct_lump_n()` keeps the most common levels and puts the rest in "Other": here {n_other} riders from the six smaller neighbourhoods. A chart with a few bars and "Other" is easier to read than one with a dozen.

steps.title: Answers that compare: ordered factors

runs.code:
survey |>
  mutate(satisfaction = ordered(satisfaction, levels = satisfaction_levels)) |>
  count(content = satisfaction >= "Satisfied")
alternatives: survey |> mutate(satisfaction = factor(satisfaction, levels = satisfaction_levels, ordered = TRUE)) |> count(content = satisfaction >= 'Satisfied')
runs.purpose: make satisfaction an ordered factor, and count the riders at Satisfied or above
runs.task: Make `satisfaction` an ordered factor with `ordered()` and `levels = satisfaction_levels`, then count the riders by `content = satisfaction >= "Satisfied"`.

steps.explain: An ordered factor's levels are ranked, so `>=` means "this answer or a better one": the count splits the riders into those at Satisfied or above and the rest, {n_satisfied} as before. With an ordinary factor, R would warn that `>=` isn't meaningful and give `NA`. Use an ordered factor when the order is part of what the answers mean, as on a scale; tibbles show it as `<ord>`.
